summary:
Chocó stands under the national framework of Colombia, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition with no surgical requirement. Consensual same-sex activity has been legal since 1981, a 2011 law bans discrimination based on sexual orientation, same-sex marriage has been available since April 2016 and joint adoption since 2015, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

In Chocó, conduct is regulated less by departmental police than by armed groups operating in the territory. Reporting on neighbouring departments describes trans women being displaced from Chocó under threat from armed actors, and CNN's August 2025 follow-up to the Sara Millerey case frames being queer in parts of the country as signing one's own death sentence, with killings continuing at the hands of armed gangs after the viral video shocked the nation.

The pattern of organised threat is documented in adjacent departments. In Caquetá, armed groups distributed flyers and WhatsApp messages naming "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets; a trans woman and local election candidate was given one week by three armed men to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night, and a second trans woman reported a friend had been killed. Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023, and discrimination confines trans women largely to hairdressing or sex work.

Nationally, the state has acknowledged conflict-driven violence as gender persecution: in July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities. The national LGBTI policy framework covers rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and bars national entities from refusing to recognise same-sex couples; protection as victims of armed conflict is the element most relevant to a visitor in Chocó.
tangentialFactors:
Chocó's risk profile is shaped by the same territorial violence documented in Caquetá and Guajira, where armed groups rather than state police set the practical rules of conduct. The Guardian's July 2024 reporting and CNN's August 2025 follow-up both describe calculated brutality persisting amid Colombia's decades-long civil conflict, a context distinct from the formal legal protections on the books.

Colombia's legal reforms have drawn international praise alongside sharp warnings. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, noting a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience.
localsOnly:
Residents of Chocó can change the sex marker on national identification by signing a document before a notary, a route open since June 2015, and national documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. Same-sex couples have been able to marry since April 2016 and adopt jointly since 2015, and a 2011 law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation.

The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture. Judgments T-314 of 2011, T-909 of 2011 and T-301 of 2004 protect entry to public and commercial premises.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory contains no Chocó-specific finding on trans safety, facilities, or local enforcement; the Chocó Department reference yielded nothing usable. Findings on armed-group threat and displacement are drawn from Caquetá and Guajira and are presented as regional pattern, not as documented incidents inside Chocó itself.

Whether the comprehensive trans law still under legislative consideration in 2025 has since been enacted is unresolved in the sources provided. The claim that trans women are being displaced from Chocó appears in secondary reporting without named cases or dates attached to Chocó specifically.
